papers.title: The multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier
papers.abstract: We prove that the multiplicative complexity of the three-bit low-half multiplier is six, giving a structural, enumeration-free lower-bound proof valid against unrestricted nonlinear reuse in Boolean XOR-AND circuits. The value was previously established by SAT searches of the second author. An explicit six-AND circuit supplies the upper bound. The lower bound combines derivatives, quadratic products, complementary minors, and extraction modulo a Boolean ideal. Independent finite checks accompany the arguments. $\mathrm{MC}(M_3)=6$ is fully formalized in Lean 4. The kernel-checked proof uses only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

papers.title: Sowing the Seeds of Intractability: Kalah is PSPACE-complete
papers.abstract: Kalah is a classic two-player game in the mancala family of sowing games. Computers have solved several standard-size starting positions, but the complexity of the game on boards of growing size has remained open. We study the natural generalization in which the number of pits per side is part of the input and an arbitrary position is given, with the stone counts given in unary. We show that deciding whether a designated player can force a win from such a position is PSPACE-complete. The hard positions have Alice to move first and both stores initially empty. The same positions are hard under either common convention for capture opposite an empty pit, and with or without the bonus rule, which gives a player another turn when the last stone is sown into their own store. We introduce Line Kalah as an intermediate problem, a game on a line in which stones that leave the line effectively disappear and Alice must save each of her target pits before Bob captures it, and we reduce quantified Boolean formulas to it. The reduction uses a set of sequential timer piles whose last stones approach a group of targets, forcing Alice to choose between two captures in order to set the truth value of a variable, and a final capture gadget to test a clause chosen by Bob (only one is needed adversarially). Since either player may move any pile at any time, the stages are placed so that premature timer firings protect earlier potential targets. For a true formula, Alice's strategy against arbitrary opposing play either gains enough time to save the remaining targets (after Bob deviates from the intended play) or reaches the final test with a correctly encoded, protected input. Finally, the line positions are embedded in Kalah with both stores empty. A separate Bob pit holds the score adjustment, so the winner takes a strict majority of the stones.

papers.title: An upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron
papers.abstract: We establish the first nontrivial upper bound on the number of edges of a Gomory corner polyhedron, resolving a long-standing open question. For an $n$-dimensional corner polyhedron associated with an integer lattice of determinant $\delta$, the number of edges is at most $$ O\left(n6^n \cdot \bigl(1+\log_2(2\delta)\bigr)^{2n-3}\right). $$ This improves the standard bound obtained by counting pairs of vertices, reducing the logarithmic exponent from $(2n-2)$ to $(2n-3)$.

papers.title: Optimal Polyomino Fences
papers.abstract: The $n$-omino fence problem asks how many cells can be surrounded by placing every $n$-omino exactly once in the grid. We present a new dynamic programming approach for this problem, allowing us to prove optimality for the pentomino and hexomino fence and to classify all possible pentomino orders by optimal area. For the first time we also provide strong heuristic solutions and upper bounds for all fences up to $n = 15$, after which we even approximate the $500$-omino fence with computational experiments. Finally, we generalize the problem to 3D, where we prove optimality for pentacubes and derive heuristic solutions for hexacubes and heptacubes.

papers.title: A linear edge bound for k-quasi-planar graphs
papers.abstract: We prove the $k$-quasi-planar graph conjecture for topological drawings. For every integer $k\ge 2$, a simple graph on $n\ge 3$ vertices admitting a drawing with no $k$ pairwise crossing edges has at most $1056(k-1)^2(n-2)$ edges. Thus the number of edges is linear in $n$, with an explicit quadratic dependence on $k$. The result allows multiple crossings between the same pair of edges, including edges with a common endpoint. The proof uses the double of a sphere with boundary to represent graph edges by closed geodesics on a hyperbolic surface. The endpoints of geodesic lifts induce partial orders of width at most $k-1$. A stability bound for greedy chain partitions, together with a counting argument over a triangulation, gives the stated edge bound.

papers.title: Resolving Tusn\'ady's Problem
papers.abstract: We prove a lower bound of $\Omega_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusn\'ady's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors. The matching upper and lower bounds are also formalized in Lean 4.

papers.title: Tripod Reordering: A 33-Queue Layout of Planar Graphs
papers.abstract: A queue layout of a graph consists of a linear order of the vertices and a partition of the edges into queues so that no two edges in a single queue are nested. The minimum number of queues needed in a queue layout of a graph is called its queue number. A planar product structure theorem of Dujmovi\'c, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt, and Wood (JACM, 2020) states that every planar graph is a subgraph of the strong product of a graph of simple treewidth at most $3$, a clique $K_3$, and a path. The result has been used to show that the queue number of planar graphs is at most $49$. Recently, Bekos, Gronemann, and Raftopoulou (Algorithmica, 2023) investigated how the general approach based on the product structure can be optimized for planar graphs. They claim that an appropriate reordering of the three vertices associated with each bag in the product structure decomposition, called a tripod, reduces the queue number of planar graphs to $42$. We first highlight a gap in their queue layout algorithm: one of the choices required by the algorithm is not guaranteed to exist. Then we show how to address the limitation and provide an alternative tripod reordering mechanism that reduces the upper bound on the queue number of planar graphs to $33$. As a corollary, bipartite planar graphs have queue number at most $22$.

papers.title: Explicit Subspace Evasive Sets via Subspace Designs
papers.abstract: Given a finite field $\mathbb F_q$, we say that a set $A\subseteq \mathbb F^n_q$ is an $(r,c)$ subspace evasive set if and only if for any affine subspace $U\subseteq \mathbb F^n_q$ with bounded dimension $\dim(U)\leq r$, the intersection size $|A\cap U|$ is at most $c$. The probabilistic method shows the existence of $(r,c)$ subspace evasive sets with $|A| = q^{(1-\epsilon) n}$ with $c = O(r/\epsilon)$. However, the best explicit constructions by Dvir--Lovett (STOC 2012) and Ben-Aroya--Shinkar (CJTCS 2013) have $c$ growing as an exponential function of $r$. Here, we give an explicit construction of such subspace evasive set that achieves the intersection bound $c=O(\min(r\log(r/\epsilon)/\epsilon, r^2/\epsilon))$ when both $r$ and $1/\epsilon$ are constants. Our approach is simple and the key idea is to compose subspace design codes (Guruswami-Xing, STOC 2013) with a suitably chosen ``local'' subspace evasive set. As a corollary, we give the first construction of an explicit (strongly) capacity-achieving list-recoverable code with nearly optimal list size, circumventing all previously-known barriers to construction.

papers.title: A polynomial-time approximation scheme for the weighted Euclidean Minimum Latency Problem in fixed dimension
papers.abstract: In the Traveling Salesman Problem, a route must visit all customers and return to its starting point while minimizing its total length. The Minimum Latency Problem, also known as the Traveling Repairman Problem, instead minimizes the sum of the times at which customers are first visited. We give a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the weighted Euclidean Minimum Latency Problem in every fixed dimension, with arbitrary nonnegative customer weights. Our proof restricts the form of a solution in three steps, each with a controlled increase in cost. First, a decomposition based on Sitters' method assigns customers to phases that start and end at the root. Second, within each phase, we divide the route into a constant number of blocks and charge each customer at the end of its assigned block. The resulting objective is a nonnegative linear combination of block lengths. Third, we add an auxiliary dimension and use a fixed Minkowski norm to close each block path into a tour. Arora's closed-tour estimate then gives paths that cross the boundaries of a common dissection only at designated portals and a bounded number of times per face. A dynamic program optimizes the restricted objective, and projecting its paths back to the original space gives the final route. Rounding weights and coordinates keeps the state space polynomial.

papers.title: Tree Decomposition of Product and Nest Graphs for Assortment Optimization under the Generalized Nested Logit Model
papers.abstract: The generalized nested logit model extends the nested logit model by allowing each product to belong to multiple nests. The overlapping nests in the generalized nested logit model can capture complex substitution patterns, and the model has found applications in many areas. We study the assortment optimization problem under the generalized nested logit model and prove that it is NP-hard when there are only two nests or when any two distinct nests have at most one product in common. Motivated by these complexity results, we introduce novel concepts of product and nest graphs that capture which products are included in which nests. We use the tree decompositions of the graphs to characterize when the assortment optimization problem admits efficient solution methods. When the treewidth of a product graph is bounded, the assortment optimization problem can be solved in polynomial time. If the treewidth of the product graph is unbounded but the treewidth of the nest graph is bounded, then there exists a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. These results represent the first polynomial-time algorithms for assortment optimization under the generalized nested logit model. Our numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the generalized nested logit model provides a better fit to the data than many existing models in the literature.

papers.title: Conflict-Free Cuts: Exploring the Boundaries of Tractability
papers.abstract: A conflict-free cut of a host graph $G$ is an edge cut containing no conflicting pair of edges. The conflicts are specified by a conflict graph $\widehat G$ whose vertex set is $E(G)$. The conflict-free cut problem asks if the given instance $(G, \widehat G)$ has a conflict-free cut. When restricted to planar $G$ and 1-regular $\widehat G$, the problem is polynomial time solvable when $G$ has maximum degree 4, but NP-complete already at maximum degree 5. We study the complexity of conflict-free cut problem under restrictions on the degrees of $G$, the components of $\widehat G$, and the locality of the conflicts. A conflict is local if its two edges share an endpoint in $G$. We prove the following results. * For $\Delta(\widehat G)\le1$, a directed-cycle formulation gives a polynomial-time algorithm when $|E(G)|\le2|V(G)|$, hence for maximum degree four. The problem is NP-complete on $5$-regular hosts with exactly $1$-regular conflicts. * For $\Delta(\widehat G)\le1$, we give a constructive FPT algorithm in $s_4(G)=\sum_v\max\{0,d_G(v)-4\}$, single-exponential for planar hosts. For arbitrary conflicts, we give an XP algorithm in $\eta=\max\{0,|E(\widehat G)|-|V(G)|\}$. * On $4$-regular hosts, local exactly $2$-regular conflicts with components $C_3,C_4$ give NP-completeness. For local conflicts at maximum degree four, pair or triangle components separately permit polynomial algorithms, but mixing them gives NP-completeness. We classify cases where $\widehat G$ is a union of cliques. * An $a$-COC is a vertex set whose deletion leaves components of order at most $a$. For local conflicts, the problem is FPT in the minimum $2$-COC size, but NP-complete with a supplied $3$-COC of size six. Without locality, hardness holds with a supplied $2$-COC of size six. Both hardness results use exactly $1$-regular conflicts.

papers.title: Constrained intersection representations and forbidden patterns
papers.abstract: We study the interplay between two types of graph classes: the ones defined by intersections of geometric objects and the ones defined by the absence of a substructure. More precisely, we study intersection graphs that are grounded, that is, the objects lie above a horizontal line that they touch, and ordered graphs with forbidden patterns, that is, ordered graphs that avoid a set of ordered induced subgraphs. These two approaches are fundamentally different, but it is known that several interesting graph classes have both types of characterizations, and we aim to understand whether this is a general phenomenon. Our contributions are the following. First, we identify a family of patterns on four vertices and a natural hierarchy of intersection graphs of strings whose classes are nicely interleaved. This raises hopes to prove connections between the two perspectives. Second, we dampen these hopes by proving that a class of (ordered) intersection graphs that we study cannot be characterized by a finite set of forbidden patterns. Third, we show a dual impossibility result: there exists a pattern-defined class of our hierarchy that admits no intersection representation, if we require this representation to be closed under natural operations such as translation and scaling. However, it turns out that if we allow slightly more exotic intersection representations, then we can find one for this pattern-defined class.

papers.title: Edge-wise Graph Alignments
papers.abstract: Pairwise graph ``alignments'', usually defined as maximum common subgraphs, have been considered in many application domains, including the comparison of molecular structures. Most commonly, the problem is formulated as maximum common induced subgraph (MCIS) or maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) problems. Sometimes these formulations are restricted to connected common subgraphs. Common subgraph problems readily generalize to more than two input graphs. However, this concept is fundamentally distinct from the notion of multiple sequence alignments. Abstractly, alignments are defined as super-structures from which the individual input objects are recovered via structure-preserving projections. While the mathematical construction readily applies to common induced subgraphs, it does not fully encompass the common edge subgraph problem, which is the variant more commonly employed in cheminformatics applications. In order to consistently define multiple edge-based alignments of graphs we represent a graph $G$ as E-graph $(E,\mathscr{V})$, where $E$ is the edge set of $G$ and $\mathscr{V}$ is the set of sets of incident edges. This representation implicitly encodes the vertices in terms of edge data. Alignments of E-graphs are themselves E-graphs that contain the input (E-)graphs as subgraphs. Maximum edge subgraphs correspond to maximum induced sub-E-graphs, and they can thus be computed using a slightly modified version of the VF2 algorithm without the need to switch from graphs to line graphs. Furthermore, multiple alignments of (E-)graphs yield a natural definition of a consensus graph that is ``on average'' present in the input without having to be a subgraph of every (and in fact of any) input graph.

papers.title: Nonlinear lower-tail large deviations at criticality
papers.abstract: We introduce general methods to derive lower tail large deviation principles, for a variety of nonlinear problems of combinatorial interest. These methods are especially effective in "critical" regimes, where the nonlinearities are not sparse enough for Poissonian lower tails (e.g., Janson's inequality does not provide a sharp tail bound), but the situation is not so dense that combinatorial effects dominate (e.g., we cannot directly apply the theory of hypergraph containers or the relative entropy framework of Kozma-Samotij). In particular, these are regimes where one expects interesting phase transitions to occur. Our results have a number of consequences related to subgraphs in random graphs, answering various questions of Warnke and Jenssen-Perkins-Potukuchi-Simkin. For example, consider a random graph $G\sim \mathbb G(n,p)$, and let $L_\triangle(n,p)=\log\Pr[G\text{ is triangle-free}]$. The first-order asymptotics of $L_\triangle(n,p)$ have long been known in all parameter ranges except the critical regime where $p$ has order of magnitude $1/\sqrt n$. We are able to fill this gap: for any fixed $c>0$, we show that $n^{-3/2}L_\triangle(n,c/\sqrt n)$ converges to a limit expressed in terms of a two-parameter variational problem, which has a single phase transition at $c\approx 4.341$. In contrast, we show that there is no such phase transition for the probability that $G$ is $C_{2\ell}$-free, for any fixed even cycle $C_{2\ell}$. We also obtain some applications in combinatorial design theory. Addressing conjectures of Glock-K\"uhn-Lo-Osthus, Kelly, and Kwan-Sah-Sawhney-Simkin, we obtain new estimates on the number of order-$n$ Steiner triple systems with no Pasch configuration and the number of order-$n$ Latin squares with no $2\times 2$ Latin subsquare (both tight up to a factor of $\exp(o(n^2))$).

papers.title: Exploring 3-CNF Formulas Generated From Partial Steiner Triple Systems
papers.abstract: Steiner triple systems (STS) and subsets of these known as partial STS (PSTS) are combinatorial objects that have received substantial interest from mathematicians since their introduction in 1847. Over the last three decades, (P)STS have found applications in diverse fields ranging from digital circuit testing to wireless transmission. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the triple in (P)STS allows for a mapping to 3-conjunctive normal form (3-CNF) formulas, the Boolean formula used as input to 3-SAT. Prompted by this ready conversion of (P)STS to 3-CNF formulas and numerous real-world applications of (P)STS, we explore the intersection of (P)STS with 3-SAT and its counting version \#3-SAT. We explain the properties of (P)STS-generated 3-CNF formulas in terms familiar to the SAT community and experimentally compare them against randomly-generated 3-CNF formulas. We find that PSTS-3-CNF formulas are statistically distinct from randomly generated 3-CNF formulas, in both probability of satisfiability and expected solution count.

papers.title: Small classes have linear neighbourhood complexity
papers.abstract: A hereditary graph class is small if it contains at most $n!c^n$ labelled graphs on $n$ vertices for some constant $c$. Small classes include proper minor-closed classes and classes of bounded twin-width. We prove that every small class has linear neighbourhood complexity, that is, in every graph in the class, vertex neighbourhoods intersect any $k$-vertex set in only $O(k)$ distinct ways. This resolves a conjecture of Bonnet, Duron, and the first two authors (ITCS 2025) and makes the algorithmic, structural, and representation consequences of linear neighbourhood complexity available for every small class. In particular, every small class admits an adjacency labelling scheme with $O(\log^2 n)$-bit labels, improving the previous $O(\log^3 n)$ bound.

papers.title: Asymptotically Optimal Bounds for Counting Near-Minimum Circuits in Regular Matroids
papers.abstract: For a regular matroid on $m$ elements with positive weights and weighted girth $g_w$, we prove that the number of circuits of weight at most $\alpha g_w$ is bounded by $(Km)^{2\alpha}$, for every real $\alpha\ge1$ and an absolute constant $K$. This improves the previous $m^{O(\alpha^2)}$ bound of Gurjar and Vishnoi and matches classic graph cut and cycle counting bounds of Karger and Subramanian. We also show this is asymptotically optimal for all real $\alpha\geq 1$ under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture, while unconditional optimality holds for half-integer $\alpha$ by prior results. As consequences, we resolve a recent conjecture by Khanna, Putterman, and Song implying the existence of a parallel basis search algorithm for regular matroids terminating in logarithmically many rounds of independence queries, and obtain improved bounds on the number of near-minimum weight codewords in regular codes and near-shortest vectors in totally unimodular lattices under $\ell_p$-norms.

papers.title: Improved Lower Bounds for Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares (MOLS) at 33 Orders
papers.abstract: A Latin square of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array over symbols $\{0,1,\ldots n-1\}$, such that the same symbol does not appear twice in any row or any column. Two Latin squares of order $n$ are orthogonal if, when superimposed, they yield each of the $n^2$ ordered pairs of symbols exactly once. A set of two or more Latin squares are mutually orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS) if each pair of distinct squares is orthogonal. Let $N(n)$ be the maximum size of a set of MOLS of order $n$. For most $n$ which are not prime powers, there is a wide gap between known upper and lower bounds on $N(n)$. This has led to interest in constructing new larger sets of MOLS for explicit values of $n$, to incrementally improve the lower bounds on $N(n)$. This paper provides MOLS that improve the lower bound on $N(n)$ for 33 values of $n$ in the range from 22 through 494. The constructions were found by GPT-6 Astra, and use established techniques including difference matrices, quasi-difference matrices, orthogonal arrays, and projective planes. A highlight is 4 MOLS of order $n=22$; combined with pre-existing results, this establishes $N(n) \geq 4$ for all $n>10$.

papers.title: Large diameter for $(\Delta+2)$-colouring reconfiguration
papers.abstract: Given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, the reconfiguration graph $\mathcal{R}_{k}(G)$ has the proper $k$-colourings of $G$ for vertices, two of which are adjacent if and only if they differ on precisely one vertex of $G$. In $2022$, Cambie, Cranston and the author proved that the diameter of $\mathcal{R}_{\Delta+2}(G)$ is at most $n+2\mu$, and put forth a collection of conjectures that in its strongest and most beautiful form would imply that the diameter of $\mathcal{R}_{\Delta+2}(G)$ is precisely equal to $n + \mu$, for every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, matching number $\mu$ and maximum degree $\Delta$. Here we disprove most of those conjectures. Our constructions have reconfiguration diameter at least $n+\frac{3}{2}\mu-2$. We also provide counterexamples that are $\Delta$-regular, we show that every graph has reconfiguration diameter at least $n+\frac{1}{2} \mu$, and we advertise an extension to hypergraphs. It is now much more mysterious how the diameter behaves, so we propose a number of open problems.

papers.title: New bounds on the boxicity of Kneser graphs
papers.abstract: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, the boxicity $\operatorname{box}(G)$ is the least integer $d$ such that $G$ is the intersection graph of axis-parallel boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The Kneser graph $K(n,k)$ is the graph whose vertex set corresponds to the family of $k$ sized subsets of an $n$ sized ground set, and a pair of vertices are adjacent if and only if the corresponding sets are disjoint. In this short paper, we provide new bounds for the boxicity of $K(n,k)$. We first show that for $k\ge 2$ and $n\ge 2k+1$, $\operatorname{box}(K(n,k))\ge n-2k$, thereby improving the lower bounds of Caoduro and Lichev [Discrete Mathematics 346(5):113333 (2023)] when $n\geq 3k+1$ and $k\ge 3$. The proof of this result uses the topological method and follows a strategy similar to Greene's proof of the Kneser's conjecture on the chromatic number of $K(n,k)$. We also show that for $k\ge 2$, $t\ge 1$ and $n=2k+t$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+t,k)) \leq O( t^3\log(2k+t) ).$ In particular, for every $t=t(k)\ge1$ with $t^3\log k=o(k)$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+t,k))=o(k)$. This is the first upper bound on the boxicity of $K(n,k)$ that is sublinear in $n$. We also show that for large enough $k$, $\operatorname{box}(K(2k+1,k))\le \frac{3\ln (2k+1)}{\ln\ln (2k+1)}$.

papers.title: Triameter, distance packings, and vertex connectivity
papers.abstract: We study upper bounds for the triameter of a connected graph in terms of distance packings and vertex connectivity. For any positive integer $k$, we bound the triameter of a graph by a linear function of its $k$-packing number and show that this bound is tight for all values of the parameters. As a corollary, we confirm the conjecture of Das and Abdio\u{g}lu on the upper bound for the triameter in terms of the order and the minimum degree of a graph. We also find the maximum triameter among graphs with given order and vertex connectivity, and describe the extremal graphs. Our main tool is a projection of a graph onto a spider or a unicyclic graph which preserves the distances between three prescribed vertices.

papers.title: Boolean combinations of graphs
papers.abstract: Boolean combinations allow combining given combinatorial objects to obtain new, potentially more complicated, objects. In this paper, we initiate a systematic study of this idea applied to graphs. In order to understand expressive power and limitations of boolean combinations in this context, we investigate how they affect different combinatorial and structural properties of graphs, in particular $\chi$-boundedness, as well as characterize the structure of boolean combinations of graphs from various classes.

papers.title: A characterization of interval nest digraphs
papers.abstract: A digraph consisting of a set of vertices $V$ and a set of arcs $E$ is called an interval digraph if there exists a family of closed intervals $\{I_u,J_u\}_{u \in V}$ such that $uv$ is an arc if and only if the intersection of $I_u$ and $J_v$ is non-empty. Interval digraphs naturally generalize interval graphs, by extending the classical interval intersection model to directed graphs. Several subclasses of interval digraphs have been studied in the literature-such as balanced, chronological and catch interval digraphs-each characterized by admitting interval representations that satisfy specific restrictions. Among these, interval nest digraphs are the ones that admit an interval representation in which $J_u$ is contained in $I_u$ for all vertices $u$ of $V$. In this work, we provide a complete characterization of interval nest digraphs in terms of vertex linear orderings with forbidden patterns, which we call nest orderings. This result completes the picture of vertex-ordering characterizations among the main subclasses of interval digraphs.

papers.title: Sharp Bounds on the Number of Small Cuts
papers.abstract: A $k$-cut of an undirected graph is a minimal edge set whose removal leaves at least $k$ connected components, and its cost is the sum of its edge costs. Write $\lambda_k$ for the minimum cost of a $k$-cut. For fixed $k\ge2$ and $\alpha\ge1$, we show that in any $n$-vertex graph with $n\ge k$ and nonnegative edge costs, the number of $k$-cuts of cost strictly below $\alpha\lambda_k$ is $O(n^{\lceil\alpha k\rceil-1})$. This implies an $O(n^{\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor})$ bound for $k$-cuts of cost at most $\alpha\lambda_k$, sharpening the $O(n^{\alpha k})$ bound of Gupta, Harris, Lee and Li. For $k=2$, our strict bound resolves a conjecture of Henzinger and Williamson and an open question of Karger. The exponent $\lceil\alpha k\rceil-1$ is optimal for $k$-cuts for every $k\ge2$ and $\alpha>1$.

papers.title: An Asymptotically Tight Bound on the Number of Distinct Squares in Circular Words
papers.abstract: A square is a word $xx$ with $x$ nonempty. We study the maximum number of distinct squares occurring in the rotations of a word of length $n$. Amit and Gawrychowski (SPIRE 2017) obtained an upper bound of $3.14n$. Charalampopoulos et al. (CPM 2026) improved the upper bound to $\lceil9n/5\rceil$ and gave a binary construction with at least $3n/2-O(\sqrt n)$ distinct squares for infinitely many $n$. They conjectured an upper bound of $3n/2$. Li and Song subsequently reported an improved upper bound of $5n/3$. We prove that a circular word of length $n$ containing $\sigma$ distinct letters has at most $\lfloor3(n-\sigma)/2\rfloor$ distinct squares. This settles the conjecture and establishes that the leading coefficient $3/2$ is optimal even for binary words. Our proof groups squares by their Lyndon roots and, for primitive words, uses a weighted count of circuits in the Rauzy graphs of the bi-infinite repetition of the word.

papers.title: An Empirical Square-Root Law for the Degree Discrepancy of Binary m-Sequences
papers.abstract: Let $k\ge 2$, $N=2^k$, $M=N-1$ and let $\Delta(r)$ be the range, over all starting offsets, of the total-variation degree discrepancy of a length-$r$ window of a primitive binary linear feedback shift register (LFSR) of period $M$. Degree-discrepancy profiles for every $k\le 28$ support the scaling $\max_r \Delta(r)=\Theta(\sqrt{N})=\Theta(2^{k/2})$. The tabulated peaks are maxima on a discrete grid, hence lower bounds on the exhaustive maximum. The normalized peaks $d_k=\max_{r\in R_k}\Delta(r)/2^{k/2}$ oscillate between values near 1/2 and values that approach, but do not exceed, 1. The data suggest $\liminf d_k=1/2$ and $\limsup d_k\le 1$. We conjecture the same square-root law for the exhaustive maximum, with those normalized envelopes. A Brownian-bridge heuristic accounts for the square-root scale. The same profiles do not place the recorded maximizer at mid-path: after folding by the complement identity $\Delta(M-r)=\Delta(r)$, the median of $\min(\rho^*_k,1-\rho^*_k)$ is 0.35, and several $k$ (notably 16 and 28) peak on a short window. Mid-horizon $\Delta$ remains a large fraction of the peak, so the square-root scale can still come from a Brownian-bridge envelope. The same range has two readings of the starting offset: a pairing fragment in serial-knockout scheduling, and a change to the plaintext on an LFSR orbit. The location of the maximizer is not part of the conjecture. Open questions that separate the conjecture from a theorem are listed.

papers.title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Riordan arrays have traditionally been studied as infinite lower-triangular matrices that encode generating-function transformations and combinatorial relationships. This note proposes a complementary direction: using Riordan arrays as structured operators in artificial intelligence and data analysis. For a data sequence with generating function $A(z)$, a Riordan array $(g(z),f(z))$ produces the transformation \[ A(z)\longmapsto g(z)A(f(z)). \] This yields a parameterized family of causal linear operators that combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing. The resulting structure may support parameter-efficient neural-network layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, invertible architectures, and models for hierarchical or recursively generated data. We explain what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, outline several possible architectures, identify theoretical and numerical challenges, and propose an initial experimental program. The aim is not to claim that Riordan arrays are appropriate for all data, but to identify settings in which their algebraic structure supplies a useful inductive bias.

papers.title: Universal optimality on finite Lee tori
papers.abstract: We study subsets of finite Lee tori that minimize pair energy among sets of the same cardinality for every discretely completely monotone potential. At half occupancy on a product of even cycles, the two checkerboards minimize both total pair energy and maximum individual energy. They are the only minimizers for every nonconstant classical completely monotone potential on $(0,\infty)$, proving the checkerboard conjecture of Bouman, Draisma, and van Leeuwaarden for this class. At the independence number of the distance one graph on $\Z_q^n$, universally optimal sets exist exactly when $q$ is even, $q=3$, $n=1$, or $(q,n)=(5,2)$. In these cases they are precisely the maximum independent sets and form a single Lee isometry class. At density $1/5$ in $\Z_5^n$, $n\ge2$, universal optimality is characterized by a weighted count of pairs at distances one and two. We prove these results using integer box occupancy bounds that strengthen Fourier linear programming and, in the quinary case, Fourier certificates with a common zero set.

papers.title: Foliations, free cores, and Terao's conjecture for seventeen lines
papers.abstract: We prove that freeness is determined by the intersection lattice for arrangements of seventeen lines in the complex projective plane. The proof reduces a possible counterexample to smaller arrangements whose realisation spaces can be computed. A minimal logarithmic derivation defines a foliation; its inflection divisor and a local singularity count imply that the non-free member of a counterexample is nearly free with exponents $(7,10)$. Deleting four lines then produces a thirteen-line arrangement whose second Chern class is controlled by a combinatorial deficit. When the deficit is four, the remaining arrangement is free with exponents $(6,6)$. An exact covering argument places the necessary thirteen-line cores in four finite classes, containing $3{,}829{,}691$ lattices. We compute their realisation spaces and reconstruct all relevant seventeen-line extensions, including specialisations of positive-dimensional families. Among the candidate lattices, exactly sixteen admit a non-free realisation; they are rigid and have no free realisation. Together with the known cases, this establishes Terao's conjecture for central arrangements of at most seventeen planes in $\mathbb{C}^3$.

papers.title: Face rings and the cohomology of unions of Schubert varieties
papers.abstract: The cohomology ring of a union of Schubert varieties $X_{W}=\bigcup_{w\in W}X_w,$ for $W\subseteq S_n$, in the complete flag variety is well known to be a quotient of the coinvariant ring $R_n$. We determine exactly when the ideal defining this quotient is generated by squarefree monomials, i.e. when it can be identified with the image of a Stanley-Reisner ideal $I_\Delta$ in $R_n$. We prove that a single Schubert variety $X_w$ has this property exactly when $w\in S_n$ avoids a set of seven patterns, and in this case we describe the corresponding doubly-pruned simplicial complex $\Delta$. We then show this is equivalent to $X_w$ being cut out of the complete flag variety by particular inclusion conditions on the pieces of the flag. We prove these complexes are vertex decomposable, and are Cohen-Macaulay precisely when $X_w$ is smooth. We then give a closed formula for the Poincar\'e polynomial of $X_w$. For unions $X_W$, pattern avoidance is necessary but no longer sufficient, and we prove a necessary and sufficient condition we call prunable that describes how the individual complexes associated to each $w\in W$ may be glued in the union. Quotients of $R_n$ by squarefree monomial ideals appear naturally in the Adams-Reiner conjecture on resolutions of Stanley-Reisner rings over certain parameter rings. We prove their conjecture for a family of simplicial complexes that includes the doubly-pruned complexes.
